decks.title: Probability — Part 1: Sample spaces and events
goals: Describe a random experiment and write its sample space (formative)
Write events as subsets and combine them with or, and, not and but not
Decide whether two events are mutually exclusive or exhaustive
Split a sample space into mutually exclusive and exhaustive events

slides.heading: Random experiments and their outcomes
slides.body_md: Before we can measure chance we must say exactly what can happen. This part builds the language: outcomes, sample spaces and events as sets.

rows: Toss a coin; on a head throw a die, on a tail toss the coin again
Draw two of the tickets 1, 2, 3, 4 one after the other, without putting the first back
Pick a pair of people from A, B, C, D (order does not matter)

visual.alt: Table of four random experiments with their sample spaces and the number of outcomes: a single coin toss has 2 outcomes; a coin followed by a die on heads or a second toss on tails has 8; two tickets drawn in order without replacement from four tickets have 12; a pair chosen from four people has 6.
visual.caption: The sample space lists every outcome once; its size is $n(S)$.

slides.narration: Welcome to probability. A random experiment is one whose result cannot be predicted in advance, such as tossing a coin or spinning a wheel. Each possible result is an outcome, and the set of all outcomes is the sample space. The table lists four experiments. A coin has two outcomes. Drawing two tickets in order from four has twelve, while choosing a pair of people from four has only six. Writing the sample space carefully is the first step of every probability question.

slides.heading: Counting the outcomes
slides.body_md: Before counting, decide two things: does the order matter, and is an item put back before the next draw? The answer changes the size of the sample space.

rows: One after the other, item put back (order matters)
One after the other, item not put back (order matters)

visual.alt: Table of three ways of choosing two items from four: with replacement and order mattering gives 16 outcomes; without replacement and order mattering gives 12; both together with order not mattering gives 6.
visual.caption: Decide whether order matters and whether items are put back before you count $n(S)$.

slides.narration: Take two items from four. If we draw one after the other and put the first back, there are sixteen outcomes. If we do not put it back, there are twelve ordered outcomes. If we pick both together and order does not matter, there are only six. So always ask whether order matters and whether items are replaced. This topic is for practice only and is not assessed in the board paper.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a two-stage experiment
slides.body_md: A coin is tossed. If it shows a head, a die is thrown; if it shows a tail, the coin is tossed again. Write the sample space.

visual.alt: Working table for the experiment of tossing a coin and then throwing a die after a head or tossing again after a tail: a head leads to six outcomes H1 to H6, a tail leads to two outcomes TH and TT, so the sample space has 8 outcomes. They are not equally likely.
visual.caption: The outcomes are not equally likely, but the sample space is still the list of all of them.

slides.narration: Follow each branch. If the coin shows a head, a die is thrown, giving six outcomes: head one up to head six. If it shows a tail, the coin is tossed again, giving two outcomes: tail head and tail tail. Together the sample space has eight outcomes. Notice that these outcomes are not equally likely, because the head branch splits into six parts while the tail branch splits into only two. We still list them all.

slides.heading: Quick check: how many events?
slides.body_md: A sample space has four outcomes. How many different events can be formed?
slides.narration: An event is any subset of the sample space. Think of choosing, for each outcome, whether it is in the event or not.

slides.heading: Events are subsets of the sample space
slides.body_md: An **event** is a subset of $S$. A **simple** (elementary) event has one outcome; a **compound** event has more. $S$ itself is the **sure** event and $\varnothing$ is the **impossible** event.

rows: The spinner shows an even number
The spinner shows a multiple of 3
The spinner shows a prime number
The spinner shows a number greater than 10
The spinner shows a number from 1 to 10

visual.alt: Table of events for a spinner numbered 1 to 10: even is 2, 4, 6, 8, 10; multiple of 3 is 3, 6, 9; prime is 2, 3, 5, 7; the number 7 alone is a simple event; a number greater than 10 is the impossible event, the empty set; any number from 1 to 10 is the sure event, the whole sample space.
visual.caption: An event is a subset of the sample space; $\varnothing$ is impossible and $S$ is sure.

slides.narration: An event is any subset of the sample space. For a spinner numbered one to ten, the event even is the set two, four, six, eight, ten. The number seven alone is a simple event. A number greater than ten cannot happen, so it is the empty set, the impossible event. Any number from one to ten is certain, so it is the whole sample space, the sure event. We say an event occurs when the outcome is a member of the set.

slides.heading: Combining events with Venn diagrams
slides.body_md: Draw the sample space as a rectangle and each event as a region. The overlap of $A$ and $B$ is $A \cap B$; the part of $A$ outside $B$ is $A - B$.

visual.alt: Venn diagram of a spinner numbered 1 to 10 with A the even numbers and B the multiples of 3. The part of A outside B holds 2, 4, 8, 10; the overlap holds 6; the part of B outside A holds 3 and 9; the region outside both circles holds 1, 5, 7.
visual.caption: The overlap holds $A \cap B = \{6\}$; the corner holds the numbers in neither event.

slides.narration: Here is the spinner again. Circle A holds the even numbers and circle B the multiples of three. The overlap holds only six, because six is both even and a multiple of three. The part of A outside B holds two, four, eight and ten. The part of B outside A holds three and nine. The corner outside both circles holds one, five and seven, the numbers in neither event.

slides.heading: The algebra of events
slides.body_md: **Or** is union, **and** is intersection, **not** is complement. "$A$ but not $B$" is $A \cap B'$, and "neither" is $A' \cap B' = (A \cup B)'$.

visual.alt: Table translating words into set symbols for even and multiple of 3 on a spinner numbered 1 to 10: A or B is 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 10; A and B is 6; not A is 1, 3, 5, 7, 9; A but not B is 2, 4, 8, 10; neither is 1, 5, 7.
visual.caption: Every English phrase about events is a set operation.

slides.narration: Every phrase about events has a set symbol. A or B means at least one happens, the union. A and B means both happen, the intersection. Not A is the complement. A but not B is the part of A outside B. Neither is the complement of the union, which also equals the intersection of the two complements. The table shows each for the even numbers and the multiples of three on the spinner.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: events on ordered pairs
slides.body_md: Two tickets are drawn in order, without replacement, from tickets $1, 2, 3, 4$. $A$: the sum is $5$. $B$: the first number is smaller than the second. List $A \cap B$ and $A \cup B$.

rows: $A$: the two numbers add up to 5
$B$: the first number is smaller than the second

visual.alt: Working table for the tickets experiment with 12 ordered pairs: event A, sum equal to 5, has 4 outcomes (1,4), (2,3), (3,2), (4,1); event B, first smaller than second, has 6 outcomes; A and B together have 2 outcomes (1,4) and (2,3); A or B has 8 outcomes.
visual.caption: List each event as a set, then take the intersection and union.

slides.narration: There are twelve ordered pairs. Event A, the sum is five, has four pairs: one four, two three, three two and four one. Event B, the first smaller than the second, has six pairs. The pairs in both are one four and two three. Taking the union, we count four plus six minus two, which is eight pairs. Listing each event as a set makes the intersection and union easy to read off.

slides.heading: Quick check: are they exclusive?
slides.body_md: True or false: when a coin is tossed twice, "two heads" and "at least one head" are mutually exclusive.
slides.narration: Write both events as sets and look for a common outcome.

slides.heading: Mutually exclusive and exhaustive events
slides.body_md: $A$ and $B$ are **mutually exclusive** if $A \cap B = \varnothing$ (they cannot happen together) and **exhaustive** if $A \cup B = S$ (one of them must happen).

visual.alt: Table of four pairs of events on a spinner numbered 1 to 10. Even and odd are both mutually exclusive and exhaustive. Even and multiple of 3 are neither. Less than 4 and greater than 7 are mutually exclusive but not exhaustive. At most 6 and at least 5 are exhaustive but not mutually exclusive.
visual.caption: Mutually exclusive: $A \cap B = \varnothing$. Exhaustive: $A \cup B = S$.

slides.narration: Two events are mutually exclusive when they have no outcome in common. They are exhaustive when together they cover the whole sample space. Even and odd are both. Even and multiple of three share six, and miss one, so they are neither. Less than four and greater than seven never overlap but leave gaps, so they are exclusive only. At most six and at least five cover everything but overlap, so they are exhaustive only.

slides.heading: A routine for classifying a pair
slides.body_md: Two set calculations settle everything: the intersection decides exclusive, the union decides exhaustive. If both hold, each event is the complement of the other.

nodes.label: Both? Then A and B are complements

visual.alt: Flow chart for classifying two events: find the intersection and call the events mutually exclusive if it is empty; find the union and call them exhaustive if it is the whole sample space; if both hold, each event is the complement of the other.
visual.caption: Two set checks settle both questions.

slides.narration: Here is a routine. First find the intersection of the two events. If it is empty, they are mutually exclusive. Then find the union. If it equals the whole sample space, they are exhaustive. If both are true, then each event is exactly the complement of the other. Following these two steps removes any guesswork when a question asks you to classify a pair of events.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: classify three pairs
slides.body_md: On $S = \{1, \ldots, 12\}$, $E_1$ is the multiples of $3$, $E_2$ the numbers leaving remainder $1$ on division by $3$, $E_3$ remainder $2$. Classify some pairs.
bullets: **$E_1, E_2$ —** no common number; union has $8$ numbers

visual.alt: Working table classifying three pairs of events on the numbers 1 to 12: E1 and E2 have an empty intersection and a union of 8 numbers, so they are mutually exclusive but not exhaustive; E1 and the multiples of 2 share 6 and 12 and their union has 8 numbers, so they are neither; the union of E1 and E2 together with E3 has an empty intersection and a union of 12 numbers, so they are mutually exclusive and exhaustive.
visual.caption: Check the intersection for exclusive and the union for exhaustive.

slides.narration: Take the numbers one to twelve. The first pair has an empty intersection, but the union has only eight numbers, so it is mutually exclusive but not exhaustive. The multiples of three and the multiples of two share six and twelve, and their union is not everything, so they are neither. Finally the union of the first two events and the third event have nothing in common and together cover all twelve numbers, so that pair is both.

slides.heading: Quick check: which pair?
slides.body_md: On a spinner numbered $1$ to $10$, $P$ is "prime", $Q$ "a multiple of $3$" and $R$ "a perfect square". Which pair is mutually exclusive?
slides.narration: List the three sets and check each pair for a common number.

slides.heading: Partitioning the sample space
slides.body_md: Events $E_1, E_2, E_3$ that are pairwise mutually exclusive and together exhaustive **partition** $S$: every outcome lies in exactly one of them.

visual.alt: The sample space drawn as a rectangle split into three vertical strips E1, E2 and E3 that do not overlap and together fill the rectangle. A circle labelled A is drawn across all three strips.
visual.caption: Mutually exclusive and exhaustive events cut $S$ into pieces: every outcome lies in exactly one.

slides.narration: Sometimes we cut the sample space into several events. If they never overlap and together fill the space, we call them a partition. In the picture, three strips cover the rectangle, and any other event, drawn as a circle, is split into pieces by the strips. Every outcome belongs to exactly one strip. This idea is powerful, because the probabilities of the strips will add to one.

slides.heading: A partition by remainders
slides.body_md: Dividing by $3$ puts each of $1, \ldots, 12$ into exactly one of three classes. Later we will add the class probabilities.

visual.alt: Table splitting the numbers 1 to 12 into three events by their remainder on division by 3: E1 is 3, 6, 9, 12; E2 is 1, 4, 7, 10; E3 is 2, 5, 8, 11. No number appears twice and all twelve numbers appear.
visual.caption: Pairwise mutually exclusive and together exhaustive: a partition of $S$.

slides.narration: Here is a concrete partition. Divide each of the numbers one to twelve by three. The remainder is zero, one or two. The three classes each hold four numbers, no number appears twice, and all twelve numbers appear. So the three events are pairwise mutually exclusive and exhaustive. Any other event, such as even numbers, is the union of its overlaps with these three classes.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: events on a code
slides.body_md: A two-digit code uses the digits $1, 2, 3$, repeats allowed. $A$: first digit smaller than second. $B$: digit sum even. Are $A$ and $B$ mutually exclusive?

rows: No: the code (1, 3) is in both

visual.alt: Working table for a two-digit code made from the digits 1, 2, 3 with repeats allowed: nine codes in all; event A, first digit smaller than the second, is (1,2), (1,3), (2,3); event B, digit sum even, is (1,1), (1,3), (2,2), (3,1), (3,3); the intersection is the single code (1,3), so A and B are not mutually exclusive.
visual.caption: Two events that share even one outcome are not mutually exclusive.

slides.narration: There are nine codes, since each digit has three choices. Event A has three codes: one two, one three and two three. Event B, the digit sum is even, has five codes: one one, one three, two two, three one and three three. The code one three is in both lists. Even a single shared outcome means the events are not mutually exclusive.

slides.heading: Quick check: counting outcomes
slides.body_md: Fill in the blank: a first speaker and a different second speaker are named from four finalists, in order. The sample space has ___ outcomes.
slides.narration: Choose the first speaker, then the second from those who remain.

slides.heading: Summary: the language of events
bullets: The sample space lists every outcome; an event is a subset.
Or, and, not, but-not and neither are union, intersection, complement and difference.
Mutually exclusive: empty intersection. Exhaustive: union is $S$.
A partition is a set of mutually exclusive and exhaustive events.

rows: A number from 1 to 10; a number above 10

visual.alt: Summary table of the language of events: the sample space is the set of all outcomes; an event is a subset; the sure event is S and the impossible event is the empty set; union, intersection and complement mean or, and, not; mutually exclusive means an empty intersection; exhaustive means the union is the whole sample space. Each has an example from the spinner numbered 1 to 10.
visual.caption: A one-page dictionary from words to sets.

slides.narration: Let us summarise. The sample space lists all outcomes and an event is a subset of it. The words or, and, not, but not and neither become union, intersection, complement, difference and the complement of the union. Mutually exclusive means an empty intersection, while exhaustive means the union is the whole sample space. A partition is a family of events that are mutually exclusive and exhaustive together.

slides.heading: Exam tips: events
bullets: **Listing (1–2 marks):** write the sample space as a set and give $n(S)$ before anything else
**Events (2 marks):** write each event as a set, then take unions and intersections
**Classifying (2 marks):** show the intersection for exclusive and the union for exhaustive
**Mistake:** treating "mutually exclusive" and "exhaustive" as the same thing
**Mistake:** writing "neither" as $A' \cup B'$ instead of $A' \cap B'$
**Mistake:** counting ordered pairs when the question says "together"
slides.narration: For questions on events, show your sets. Write the sample space first, then each event as a set, then the union or intersection. When asked to classify a pair, justify with the intersection for exclusive and the union for exhaustive. Three slips to avoid: confusing mutually exclusive with exhaustive, writing neither as the union of the complements instead of the intersection, and counting ordered pairs when the question picks items together.

decks.title: Probability — Part 2: The axiomatic approach
goals: State the three axioms and use them to assign and test probabilities
Find probabilities of events with equally likely and with weighted outcomes
Use P(not A) = 1 − P(A) and the addition theorem for P(A or B)
Solve problems on neither, A but not B and exactly one of two events

slides.heading: From counting to rules
slides.body_md: Counting favourable outcomes is not always possible. The axiomatic approach gives a few rules that every probability must obey, and everything else follows from them.

nodes.label: Is the sample space equally likely?
Want not A? Use 1 minus P(A)
Want A or B? Use the addition theorem
A and B exclusive? Drop the overlap

visual.alt: Flow chart for choosing a method: if outcomes are equally likely, count favourable over total, otherwise use the given or weighted probabilities; for not A use one minus P of A; for A or B use the addition theorem; if A and B are mutually exclusive the overlap term is zero.
visual.caption: Pick counting or weights first, then the rule for the event you need.

slides.narration: In the first part we built the language of events. Now we measure how likely they are. Sometimes outcomes are equally likely and we can count. Sometimes they are not, and the probabilities are given. The axiomatic approach covers both with three simple rules. From them we will prove everything we need. The chart shows the road map: choose counting or given probabilities, then use the rule for not A or for A or B.

slides.heading: The three axioms
slides.body_md: A probability $P$ assigns to each event a number so that $P(E) \ge 0$, $P(S) = 1$, and $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B)$ whenever $A \cap B = \varnothing$.

rows: No event has a negative probability
Something in the sample space is certain to happen
Probabilities of mutually exclusive events add

visual.alt: Table of the three axioms of probability: every event has a probability of at least zero; the probability of the whole sample space is one; and for mutually exclusive events the probability of the union is the sum of the probabilities.
visual.caption: Everything else in the chapter follows from these three statements.

math: P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B),\ A \cap B = \varnothing
slides.narration: A probability assigns each event a number obeying three axioms. First, it is never negative. Second, the whole sample space has probability one. Third, for mutually exclusive events, the probability of the union is the sum of the probabilities. The last axiom extends to any number of mutually exclusive events. Every other rule in this chapter is a consequence of these three statements.

slides.heading: Assigning probabilities to outcomes
slides.body_md: List the elementary events and give each a probability, so that every probability is non-negative and the total is $1$. The probability of an event is the sum over its outcomes.

visual.alt: Table of a probability model with four outcomes a, b, c, d with probabilities 0.15, 0.25, x and 2x. The total must equal one, so 0.4 plus 3x equals 1 and x equals 0.2, giving the probabilities 0.15, 0.25, 0.2 and 0.4.
visual.caption: The elementary probabilities must add up to $1$.

slides.narration: To build a probability model, give each elementary event a probability. They must be non-negative and add to one. In this table, outcomes a and b have probabilities zero point one five and zero point two five, and the other two are x and two x. The total must be one, so zero point four plus three x equals one, and x is zero point two. The probability of any event is then the sum over its outcomes.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: find the unknown
slides.body_md: Four outcomes have probabilities $0.15$, $0.25$, $x$ and $2x$. Find $x$ and $P(\{a, c\})$, where $a$ has $0.15$ and $c$ has $x$.

visual.alt: Working table: the four probabilities 0.15, 0.25, x and 2x add to one, so 0.4 plus 3x is 1 and x is 0.2; the probabilities are then 0.15, 0.25, 0.2 and 0.4, and the event made of outcomes a and c has probability 0.35.
visual.caption: Use axiom 2 to find the unknown, then axiom 3 to add.

slides.narration: The probabilities must add to one. So zero point one five, plus zero point two five, plus x, plus two x, equals one. That gives three x equals zero point six, so x is zero point two. The four probabilities are zero point one five, zero point two five, zero point two and zero point four. The event made of outcomes a and c has probability zero point one five plus zero point two, which is zero point three five.

slides.heading: Quick check: can they be exclusive?
slides.body_md: True or false: two events with probabilities $0.55$ and $0.6$ can be mutually exclusive.
slides.narration: If they were exclusive, the probability of the union would be the sum. Is that possible?

slides.heading: Equally likely outcomes
slides.body_md: If all $n(S)$ outcomes are equally likely, the axioms give $P(E) = \dfrac{n(E)}{n(S)}$. This is a special case of the axiom approach.

visual.alt: Table of probabilities on a spinner numbered 1 to 10 with equally likely outcomes: even has 5 favourable outcomes, probability one half; multiple of 3 has 3, probability three tenths; prime has 4, probability two fifths; even and a multiple of 3 has 1, probability one tenth.
visual.caption: With equally likely outcomes, $P(E) = \dfrac{n(E)}{n(S)}$: a special case of the axioms.

slides.narration: When every outcome is equally likely, each has probability one over the number of outcomes, and adding them up gives the familiar rule: the probability of an event is the number of favourable outcomes over the total. On the spinner, even has five favourable out of ten, so one half. Multiple of three has three, so three tenths. Prime has four, so two fifths. Even and a multiple of three has one, so one tenth.

slides.heading: Consequences of the axioms
slides.body_md: The impossible event has probability $0$; $P(A') = 1 - P(A)$ because $A$ and $A'$ are exclusive with union $S$; and every probability lies between $0$ and $1$.

headers: Check: toss a coin four times, $A$ = at least one head

visual.alt: Table of consequences of the axioms: the impossible event has probability zero; the probability of not A is one minus the probability of A because A and not A are mutually exclusive and make up the whole sample space; every probability lies between zero and one. Checked by tossing a coin four times, where at least one head has probability fifteen sixteenths and no head has one sixteenth.
visual.caption: Count the complement when "at least one" is awkward to count directly.

slides.narration: From the axioms we get three results. The impossible event has probability zero. The probability of not A is one minus the probability of A, because A and not A are mutually exclusive and together make the whole sample space, so their probabilities add to one. And every probability lies between zero and one. The table checks these for four coin tosses, where no head has probability one sixteenth.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: at least one head
slides.body_md: A coin is tossed four times. Find the probability of at least one head.

rows: "at least one head"; counting it directly is long

visual.alt: Working table for tossing a coin four times: 16 outcomes in all; the event at least one head is awkward to count, but its complement, no head, is the single outcome tails tails tails tails with probability one sixteenth; so the probability of at least one head is one minus one sixteenth, which is fifteen sixteenths.
visual.caption: When "at least one" is hard to count, count "none" and subtract from $1$.

slides.narration: There are sixteen equally likely outcomes. Counting the outcomes with at least one head directly would be long. The complement is easy: no head means all tails, a single outcome, with probability one sixteenth. So the probability of at least one head is one minus one sixteenth, which is fifteen sixteenths. Whenever you see at least one, think of the complement.

slides.heading: Quick check: not an event
slides.body_md: An imagined tea stall runs out of milk before noon with probability $\dfrac{5}{18}$. What is the probability that it does not?
slides.narration: Use the complement rule.

slides.heading: The addition theorem
slides.body_md: For any two events, $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)$. The overlap is counted in both $P(A)$ and $P(B)$, so it is subtracted once.

visual.alt: Venn diagram of two overlapping events with probabilities written in each region: A alone 0.32, both A and B 0.16, B alone 0.19, and neither event 0.33. The four regions add up to 1.
visual.caption: $P(A) = 0.32 + 0.16$, $P(B) = 0.19 + 0.16$, and the four regions add to $1$.

math: P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)
slides.narration: This Venn diagram shows probabilities in each region. A alone is zero point three two, both is zero point one six, B alone is zero point one nine, and neither is zero point three three. They add to one. The probability of A is the first two regions, and B is the middle two. If we just add P of A and P of B, the middle region is counted twice, so we subtract it once. That is the addition theorem.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: from given probabilities
slides.body_md: $P(A) = 0.48$, $P(B) = 0.35$, $P(A \cap B) = 0.16$. Find $P(A \cup B)$, $P(\text{neither})$, $P(A \text{ but not } B)$ and $P(\text{exactly one})$.

visual.alt: Working table for P(A) 0.48, P(B) 0.35 and P(A and B) 0.16: the probability of A or B is 0.67; neither is 0.33; A but not B is 0.32; exactly one of the two is 0.51.
visual.caption: Subtract the overlap once: it was counted in both $P(A)$ and $P(B)$.

slides.narration: Apply the theorem: zero point four eight plus zero point three five minus zero point one six is zero point six seven. Neither is the complement, one minus zero point six seven, which is zero point three three. A but not B removes the overlap from P of A: zero point four eight minus zero point one six, which is zero point three two. Exactly one is the union minus the overlap, zero point six seven minus zero point one six, which is zero point five one.

slides.heading: Quick check: add and subtract
slides.body_md: Fill in the blank: $P(E) = 0.28$, $P(F) = 0.43$ and $P(E \cap F) = 0.1$. Then $P(E \cup F) = $ ___.
slides.narration: Add the two probabilities and subtract the overlap once.

slides.heading: Mutually exclusive events: nothing to subtract
slides.body_md: If $A \cap B = \varnothing$ then $P(A \cap B) = 0$ and the theorem reduces to $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B)$. If they are also exhaustive, $P(A) + P(B) = 1$.

visual.alt: Table of the simpler rules for mutually exclusive events: the probability of A or B is the sum, for example 0.26 plus 0.47 is 0.73; the probability of neither is one minus that, 0.27; if the two events are also exhaustive their probabilities add to one, for example 0.4 plus 0.6.
visual.caption: No overlap means nothing to subtract.

slides.narration: When the events are mutually exclusive, the overlap is empty, so its probability is zero and the theorem becomes a simple sum. For example, zero point two six plus zero point four seven is zero point seven three, and neither has probability zero point two seven. If the two events are also exhaustive, their probabilities add to exactly one, so each is the complement of the other.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: check by counting
slides.body_md: Two dice are thrown. $A$: the numbers differ by at most $1$. $B$: the sum is $4$, $8$ or $12$. Find $P(A \cup B)$ and check by counting.

rows: $A$: the numbers differ by at most 1

visual.alt: Working table for two dice thrown together: event A, the numbers differ by at most 1, has 16 outcomes; event B, the sum is 4, 8 or 12, has 9; both together have the 3 doubles (2,2), (4,4), (6,6); the addition theorem gives 16 plus 9 minus 3 over 36, which is 22 over 36, or 11 over 18, and counting the union directly gives 22 outcomes as well.
visual.caption: The theorem and the direct count agree.

slides.narration: Two dice give thirty-six outcomes. Event A has sixteen: six doubles and ten pairs that differ by exactly one. Event B has nine: three with sum four, five with sum eight and one with sum twelve. Both together are the three doubles two two, four four and six six. The theorem gives sixteen plus nine minus three over thirty-six, which is twenty-two over thirty-six, or eleven eighteenths. Counting the union directly also gives twenty-two outcomes.

slides.heading: Quick check: find the overlap
slides.body_md: For two events, $P(A) = 0.64$, $P(B) = 0.41$ and $P(A \cup B) = 0.83$. Find $P(A \cap B)$.
slides.narration: Rearrange the addition theorem to isolate the overlap.

slides.heading: Is an assignment valid?
slides.body_md: A list of probabilities for the elementary events is valid exactly when no entry is negative and the total is $1$. Test both conditions.

slides.heading: Summary: rules of probability
bullets: Axioms: $P(E) \ge 0$, $P(S) = 1$, and additivity for exclusive events.
Addition theorem: $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)$.
Neither: $1 - P(A \cup B)$. A but not B: $P(A) - P(A \cap B)$.

The probability of not A is one minus the probability of A. The addition theorem gives the probability of A or B. From it, neither is one minus the union, and A but not B is P of A minus the overlap. slides.heading: Exam tips: probability
bullets: **Equally likely (2–3 marks):** write $n(S)$, list or count $n(E)$, then divide
**Addition theorem (3 marks):** state it, substitute each value, then simplify
**Unknown $x$ (2–3 marks):** make the total equal to $1$ first
**Mistake:** adding $P(A)$ and $P(B)$ without subtracting the overlap
**Mistake:** "neither" as $1 - P(A) - P(B)$ without adding back the overlap

For the addition theorem, state it, substitute each value and simplify. When an unknown appears in a list of probabilities, first make the total equal to one. Common slips are forgetting to subtract the overlap, accepting an answer above one or below zero, and computing neither without adding back the overlap.

sections.heading: 1. Random experiments and sample spaces (formative)
sections.body_md:
A **random experiment** has several possible results and the result cannot be predicted in advance. Each result is an **outcome**, and the set of all outcomes is the **sample space** $S$.

Write $S$ as a set and state $n(S)$. For a two-stage experiment follow each branch. Decide whether order matters and whether items are replaced: choosing $2$ from $4$ gives $16$ outcomes with replacement and order, $12$ without replacement but in order, and $6$ when the two are picked together.

Outcomes need not be equally likely; the sample space still lists all of them.

key_terms.definition_md: An experiment whose result is not certain beforehand.
The set $S$ of all possible outcomes.
One possible result of the experiment.

sections.heading: 2. Events
sections.body_md:
An **event** is a subset of the sample space. An event **occurs** when the outcome is one of its members. A **simple** (elementary) event has one outcome and a **compound** event has more. The whole space $S$ is the **sure** event; the empty set $\varnothing$ is the **impossible** event.

If $S$ has $n$ outcomes there are $2^n$ events, counting $S$ and $\varnothing$. For a spinner numbered $1$ to $10$, "even" is $\{2, 4, 6, 8, 10\}$ and "greater than $10$" is $\varnothing$.

sections.heading: 3. Algebra of events
sections.body_md:
With events $A$ and $B$ of the same sample space: **$A$ or $B$** is $A \cup B$ (at least one occurs); **$A$ and $B$** is $A \cap B$; **not $A$** is $A'$; **$A$ but not $B$** is $A - B = A \cap B'$; **neither** is $A' \cap B' = (A \cup B)'$.

A Venn diagram with the sample space as a rectangle shows every region. For the even numbers and the multiples of $3$ on a spinner numbered $1$ to $10$: $A \cup B = \{2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 10\}$, $A \cap B = \{6\}$ and the neither-event is $\{1, 5, 7\}$.

visual.alt: Venn diagram of a spinner numbered 1 to 10 with A the even numbers and B the multiples of 3. The part of A outside B holds 2, 4, 8, 10; the overlap holds 6; the part of B outside A holds 3 and 9; the region outside both circles holds 1, 5, 7.
visual.caption: The overlap holds $A \cap B = \{6\}$; the corner holds the numbers in neither event.

visuals.alt: Table translating words into set symbols for even and multiple of 3 on a spinner numbered 1 to 10: A or B is 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 10; A and B is 6; not A is 1, 3, 5, 7, 9; A but not B is 2, 4, 8, 10; neither is 1, 5, 7.
visuals.caption: Every English phrase about events is a set operation.

sections.heading: 4. Mutually exclusive and exhaustive events
sections.body_md:
$A$ and $B$ are **mutually exclusive** if $A \cap B = \varnothing$: they cannot occur together. They are **exhaustive** if $A \cup B = S$: at least one must occur. Both together means each is the complement of the other.

Events $E_1, E_2, \ldots, E_n$ that are pairwise mutually exclusive and together exhaustive form a **partition** of $S$. Dividing the numbers $1$ to $12$ by $3$ gives such a partition by remainders $0, 1, 2$.

To classify a pair, find the intersection (empty?) and the union (equal to $S$?).

sections.heading: 5. The axiomatic approach
sections.body_md:
A **probability** $P$ assigns a number to each event so that: **(1)** $P(E) \ge 0$; **(2)** $P(S) = 1$; **(3)** $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B)$ whenever $A \cap B = \varnothing$.

To define a model, give each elementary event a probability: all non-negative, total $1$. The probability of an event is the sum of the probabilities of its outcomes. If an unknown such as $x$ appears, make the total equal to $1$ first.

A proposed list is **valid** exactly when no entry is negative and the total is $1$.

key_terms.definition_md: Non-negative; $P(S) = 1$; additive for mutually exclusive events.
The probability given to a single outcome; they add to 1.

formulas.latex: P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B),\ A \cap B = \varnothing

visuals.caption: A valid assignment has no negative entry and total exactly $1$.

sections.heading: 6. Equally likely outcomes and the complement
sections.body_md:
If all $n(S)$ outcomes are equally likely, each has probability $\dfrac{1}{n(S)}$ and $P(E) = \dfrac{n(E)}{n(S)}$. This is a special case of the axioms.

From the axioms: $P(\varnothing) = 0$; $P(A') = 1 - P(A)$ (since $A$, $A'$ are exclusive with union $S$); and $0 \le P(E) \le 1$. Use the complement when "at least one" is hard to count: for four coin tosses $P(\text{at least one head}) = 1 - \dfrac{1}{16} = \dfrac{15}{16}$.

key_terms.definition_md: Every outcome has the same probability.

visual.alt: Table of probabilities on a spinner numbered 1 to 10 with equally likely outcomes: even has 5 favourable outcomes, probability one half; multiple of 3 has 3, probability three tenths; prime has 4, probability two fifths; even and a multiple of 3 has 1, probability one tenth.

visuals.caption: When "at least one" is hard to count, count "none" and subtract from $1$.

sections.heading: 7. The addition theorem
sections.body_md:
For any two events: $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)$. The outcomes of $A \cap B$ are in both $P(A)$ and $P(B)$, so the overlap is subtracted once.

Related results: $P(\text{neither}) = 1 - P(A \cup B)$; $P(A \cap B') = P(A) - P(A \cap B)$; $P(\text{exactly one}) = P(A \cup B) - P(A \cap B)$. For mutually exclusive events the overlap is $0$, so $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B)$; if they are also exhaustive the two probabilities add to $1$.

For a set of equally likely outcomes, verify by counting: $n(A \cup B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A \cap B)$.

sections.heading: 8. Choosing a method
sections.body_md:
First decide whether the outcomes are equally likely: if yes, count $n(E)$ and $n(S)$; if not, use the given or weighted probabilities and add. Then pick the rule for the event wanted: not $A$ uses the complement; $A$ or $B$ uses the addition theorem; neither, $A$ but not $B$ and exactly one all come from $P(A \cup B)$ and $P(A \cap B)$.

Always check that every probability is between $0$ and $1$, and that exclusive, exhaustive events have probabilities adding to $1$.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How marks are awarded**
- *Sample space and events (1–2 marks):* write $S$ as a set with $n(S)$ and each event as a set.
- *Classifying events (2 marks):* show the intersection for mutually exclusive and the union for exhaustive.
- *Equally likely outcomes (2–3 marks):* give $n(S)$, $n(E)$ and the fraction.
- *Addition theorem (3 marks):* state it, substitute each value, simplify.
- *Axioms and assignments (2–3 marks):* make the total $1$, check no entry is negative.
- *Long answers (5 marks):* list the events, count, apply the theorem and verify by direct count.

**Common mistakes**
1. Confusing mutually exclusive with exhaustive.
2. Writing "neither" as $A' \cup B'$.
3. Adding $P(A)$ and $P(B)$ and forgetting the overlap.
4. Counting ordered pairs when items are chosen together.
5. Accepting a probability above $1$ or below $0$.
6. Not making the total $1$ before solving for an unknown.
7. Forgetting to subtract the overlap again when finding "exactly one".

cards.front_md: What is a random experiment?
cards.back_md: An experiment with several possible results where the result cannot be predicted beforehand.

cards.front_md: What is a sample space?
cards.back_md: The set $S$ of all possible outcomes of a random experiment.

cards.front_md: Name three ways of choosing 2 items from 4 and the number of outcomes.
cards.back_md: With replacement, in order: 16. Without replacement, in order: 12. Both together: 6.

cards.front_md: What is an event?
cards.back_md: A subset of the sample space. It occurs when the outcome is a member of the subset.

cards.front_md: Define simple and compound events.
cards.back_md: A simple (elementary) event has one outcome; a compound event has more than one.

cards.front_md: What are the sure and impossible events?
cards.back_md: The sure event is $S$ itself; the impossible event is $\varnothing$.

cards.front_md: How many events does a sample space with $n$ outcomes have?
cards.back_md: $2^n$ (all subsets, including $S$ and $\varnothing$).

cards.front_md: What do $A \cup B$ and $A \cap B$ mean in words?
cards.back_md: $A \cup B$: $A$ or $B$ (at least one). $A \cap B$: $A$ and $B$ (both).

cards.front_md: What is the event $A'$?
cards.back_md: "Not $A$": the outcomes of $S$ that are not in $A$.

cards.front_md: How is "$A$ but not $B$" written?
cards.back_md: $A - B = A \cap B'$.

cards.front_md: How is "neither $A$ nor $B$" written?
cards.back_md: $A' \cap B' = (A \cup B)'$. It is not $A' \cup B'$.

cards.front_md: When are two events mutually exclusive?
cards.back_md: When $A \cap B = \varnothing$: they cannot happen together.

cards.front_md: When are two events exhaustive?
cards.back_md: When $A \cup B = S$: at least one of them must happen.

cards.front_md: What is a partition of the sample space?
cards.back_md: A set of events that are pairwise mutually exclusive and together exhaustive: every outcome lies in exactly one.

cards.front_md: Are mutually exclusive events always exhaustive?
cards.back_md: No. Multiples of $3$ and multiples of $5$ on a spinner $1$ to $10$ do not overlap but miss most numbers.

cards.front_md: State the three axioms of probability.
cards.back_md: $P(E) \ge 0$; $P(S) = 1$; $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B)$ when $A \cap B = \varnothing$.

cards.front_md: When is a list of probabilities for the outcomes valid?
cards.back_md: When no entry is negative and the total is exactly 1.

cards.front_md: How do you find an unknown $x$ in a list of probabilities?
cards.back_md: Set the total of all the probabilities equal to $1$ and solve, then check no value is negative.

cards.front_md: What is the probability of an event when outcomes are equally likely?
cards.back_md: $P(E) = \dfrac{n(E)}{n(S)}$.

cards.front_md: What is the probability of an event with weighted outcomes?
cards.back_md: The sum of the probabilities of the outcomes in the event.

cards.front_md: What is $P(\varnothing)$ and why?
cards.back_md: $0$. Since $\varnothing \cup \varnothing = \varnothing$ with empty overlap, $P(\varnothing) = P(\varnothing) + P(\varnothing)$.

cards.front_md: State and prove the complement rule.
cards.back_md: $P(A') = 1 - P(A)$: $A$ and $A'$ are mutually exclusive with union $S$, so $P(A) + P(A') = P(S) = 1$.

cards.front_md: When is the complement rule the quickest method?
cards.back_md: When "at least one" is hard to count: for four coin tosses $1 - \dfrac{1}{16} = \dfrac{15}{16}$.

cards.front_md: State the addition theorem.
cards.back_md: $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)$.

cards.front_md: What is the addition theorem for mutually exclusive events?
cards.back_md: $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B)$, because $P(A \cap B) = 0$.

cards.front_md: How do you find $P(\text{neither } A \text{ nor } B)$?
cards.back_md: $1 - P(A \cup B)$.

cards.front_md: How do you find $P(A \text{ but not } B)$?
cards.back_md: $P(A \cap B') = P(A) - P(A \cap B)$.

cards.front_md: How do you find $P(\text{exactly one of } A, B)$?
cards.back_md: $P(A \cup B) - P(A \cap B)$.

cards.front_md: Why is $P(A \cup B) \le P(A) + P(B)$ always true?
cards.back_md: The addition theorem subtracts a non-negative overlap $P(A \cap B)$ from the sum.

cards.front_md: Two events have probabilities 0.55 and 0.6. Can they be mutually exclusive?
cards.back_md: No: the probability of their union would be 1.15, more than 1.

questions.stem_md: A random experiment has a sample space with exactly four outcomes. Counting the sure event and the impossible event, the number of different events that can be described is
questions.solution_md: An event is any subset of $S$. A set with $4$ elements has $2^4 = 16$ subsets, including $S$ itself and the empty set. Option (b) leaves out the empty set.

questions.stem_md: On a spinner numbered $1$ to $10$, let $P$ be "the number is prime", $Q$ "the number is a multiple of $3$" and $R$ "the number is a perfect square". Which pair of these events is mutually exclusive?
questions.solution_md: $P = \{2, 3, 5, 7\}$, $Q = \{3, 6, 9\}$, $R = \{1, 4, 9\}$. Then $P \cap Q = \{3\}$ and $Q \cap R = \{9\}$ are not empty, but $P \cap R = \varnothing$.

questions.stem_md: For any two events $A$ and $B$ of the same sample space, the probability that at least one of them occurs is
questions.solution_md: The outcomes of $A \cap B$ are counted in both $P(A)$ and $P(B)$, so the overlap is subtracted once: $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)$.

questions.stem_md: An imagined tea stall runs out of milk before noon with probability $\dfrac{5}{18}$ on a given day. The probability that it does not run out of milk before noon is
Two events $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive and exhaustive, and $P(A)$ is twice $P(B)$. Then $P(B)$ equals
questions.solution_md: Exclusive and exhaustive gives $P(A) + P(B) = 1$. With $P(A) = 2P(B)$ this reads $3P(B) = 1$, so $P(B) = \dfrac{1}{3}$.

questions.stem_md: For two events of one experiment, $P(A) = 0.45$, $P(B) = 0.3$ and $P(A \cap B) = 0.12$. The probability that $A$ or $B$ occurs is
questions.solution_md: $P(A \cup B) = 0.45 + 0.3 - 0.12 = 0.63$. Adding the three numbers gives $0.87$, and ignoring the overlap gives $0.75$; both are wrong.

questions.stem_md: If $P(A) = \dfrac{1}{2}$, $P(B) = \dfrac{2}{3}$ and $P(A \cup B) = \dfrac{5}{6}$, the probability $P(A \cap B)$ is

questions.stem_md: A school club (imagined) picks a committee of $3$ members together from $7$ members, every committee being equally likely. Find, as a decimal correct to $3$ places, the probability that two particular members, Mira and Naveen, are both on the committee.

$A$ and $A'$ are mutually exclusive and $A \cup A' = S$. By axiom 3, $P(A) + P(A') = P(S) = 1$, so $P(A') = 1 - P(A)$.

For $P(A) = \dfrac{7}{12}$: $P(A') = 1 - \dfrac{7}{12} = \dfrac{5}{12}$.

questions.solution_md: Split S into A and its complement and add their probabilities.

answer.model_answer_md:
Mutually exclusive, so $P(A \cup B) = 0.26 + 0.47 = 0.73$.

$A' \cap B' = (A \cup B)'$, so $P(A' \cap B') = 1 - 0.73 = 0.27$.

questions.solution_md: For exclusive events the overlap term is zero.

questions.stem_md: $A$, $B$ and $C$ are three events of one experiment. Using set symbols, write (a) "$A$ occurs but neither $B$ nor $C$ occurs" and (b) "none of the three events occurs".

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $A$ occurs, $B$ does not and $C$ does not: $A \cap B' \cap C'$, which is the same as $A - (B \cup C)$.

(b) None occurs: $A' \cap B' \cap C'$, which equals $(A \cup B \cup C)'$.

questions.solution_md: Say each condition as a set and join the conditions with intersection.

questions.stem_md: Two fair dice are thrown together. Let $A$ be "both numbers are prime" and $B$ "the sum of the numbers is at least $8$". Find $P(A \cup B)$.

answer.model_answer_md:
$n(S) = 36$. The prime numbers on a die are $2, 3, 5$, so $n(A) = 3 \times 3 = 9$. A sum of $8, 9, 10, 11, 12$ occurs in $5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 15$ ways, so $n(B) = 15$.

Both prime and sum at least $8$: $(3, 5), (5, 3), (5, 5)$, so $n(A \cap B) = 3$.

$P(A \cup B) = \dfrac{9 + 15 - 3}{36} = \dfrac{21}{36} = \dfrac{7}{12}$.

questions.solution_md: Count each event and the overlap, then use the addition theorem.

questions.stem_md: Two fair dice are thrown together. By counting the complement, find the probability that at least one of them shows a $6$, and list the outcomes in which exactly one die shows $6$ as a check.

answer.model_answer_md:
$P(\text{no six}) = \dfrac{5 \times 5}{36} = \dfrac{25}{36}$, because each die has $5$ faces other than $6$.

$P(\text{at least one six}) = 1 - \dfrac{25}{36} = \dfrac{11}{36}$.

Check: exactly one six gives $(6, 1), (6, 2), (6, 3), (6, 4), (6, 5), (1, 6), (2, 6), (3, 6), (4, 6), (5, 6)$, that is $10$ outcomes; adding the outcome $(6, 6)$ gives $11$.

questions.solution_md: Counting the complement avoids listing every outcome that contains a six.

marking_scheme.step: Check: 10 outcomes with exactly one six plus (6, 6) is 11

questions.stem_md: A lopsided spinner has five outcomes with probabilities $P(a) = 0.12$, $P(b) = 0.28$, $P(c) = 0.2$, $P(d) = 0.25$ and $P(e) = 0.15$. For the events $A = \{a, c, e\}$ and $B = \{b, c, d\}$, find $P(A \cup B)$ and say what the answer tells you about $A$ and $B$.

answer.model_answer_md:
$P(A) = 0.12 + 0.2 + 0.15 = 0.47$ and $P(B) = 0.28 + 0.2 + 0.25 = 0.73$. The only common outcome is $c$, so $P(A \cap B) = 0.2$.

$P(A \cup B) = 0.47 + 0.73 - 0.2 = 1$.

The union has probability $1$ and contains every outcome, so $A$ and $B$ are exhaustive (they are not mutually exclusive).

questions.solution_md: Add the elementary probabilities inside each event, then apply the addition theorem.

questions.stem_md: Three students propose probabilities for the four outcomes $x, y, z, w$ of a spinner. (i) $0.2, 0.3, 0.4, 0.2$ (ii) $0.5, 0.3, 0.3, -0.1$ (iii) $0.1, 0.4, 0.2, 0.3$. Which proposals are valid probability assignments? Give a reason for each.

answer.model_answer_md:
A valid assignment has no negative entry and total exactly $1$.

(i) $0.2 + 0.3 + 0.4 + 0.2 = 1.1 \ne 1$: not valid.

(ii) $0.5 + 0.3 + 0.3 - 0.1 = 1$, but $-0.1 < 0$ breaks axiom 1: not valid.

(iii) $0.1 + 0.4 + 0.2 + 0.3 = 1$ and every entry is at least $0$: valid.

questions.solution_md: Test both conditions, non-negative entries and total one, for every list.

questions.stem_md: For two events $A$ and $B$ of one experiment, show that $P(A \cap B) \ge P(A) + P(B) - 1$. Hence find the least possible value of $P(A \cap B)$ when $P(A) = 0.7$ and $P(B) = 0.6$.

answer.model_answer_md:
By the addition theorem, $P(A \cap B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cup B)$. Since $P(A \cup B) \le 1$, subtracting it removes at most $1$, so $P(A \cap B) \ge P(A) + P(B) - 1$.

For $P(A) = 0.7$ and $P(B) = 0.6$: $P(A \cap B) \ge 0.7 + 0.6 - 1 = 0.3$. The least possible value is $0.3$.

questions.solution_md: Use the largest value P(A or B) can take, which is 1.

marking_scheme.step: P(A and B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A or B)
P(A or B) is at most 1, so the inequality follows

questions.stem_md: A coin is tossed four times and the faces are written in order. List the outcomes of the event "exactly two heads", and find its probability and the probability of its complement.

answer.model_answer_md:
The sample space has $2^4 = 16$ equally likely outcomes.

Exactly two heads: $\text{HHTT}, \text{HTHT}, \text{HTTH}, \text{THHT}, \text{THTH}, \text{TTHH}$, which is $6$ outcomes.

$P(\text{exactly two heads}) = \dfrac{6}{16} = \dfrac{3}{8}$ and the complement has probability $1 - \dfrac{3}{8} = \dfrac{5}{8}$.

questions.solution_md: Position the two heads among the four places, then divide by the size of S.

questions.stem_md: Two different digits are chosen from $\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5\}$ one after the other and written as an ordered pair. Let $A$ be "the sum of the digits is even" and $B$ "the first digit is smaller than the second". Find $P(A \cup B)$.

answer.model_answer_md:
$n(S) = 5 \times 4 = 20$.

Sum even means both odd or both even: $3 \times 2 + 2 \times 1 = 8$, so $n(A) = 8$. The first smaller than the second happens for half of the ordered pairs, so $n(B) = 10$.

Both: $(1, 3), (1, 5), (3, 5), (2, 4)$, so $n(A \cap B) = 4$. Then $P(A \cup B) = \dfrac{8 + 10 - 4}{20} = \dfrac{14}{20} = \dfrac{7}{10}$.

questions.solution_md: Use pairs of equal parity to count A, and the symmetry of ordered pairs to count B.

marking_scheme.step: n(A and B) = 4 with the four pairs listed

questions.stem_md: Each letter of the word STATISTICS is written on its own card and one of the $10$ cards is drawn at random. Let $A$ be "the card shows a vowel" and $B$ "the card shows T". Show that $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive, and find $P(A \cup B)$ and $P(A' \cap B')$.

answer.model_answer_md:
The vowels are $A, I, I$, so $n(A) = 3$; the letter T appears $3$ times, so $n(B) = 3$. No card shows both a vowel and the letter T, so $A \cap B = \varnothing$: the events are mutually exclusive.

$P(A \cup B) = \dfrac{3}{10} + \dfrac{3}{10} = \dfrac{3}{5}$.

$P(A' \cap B') = 1 - \dfrac{3}{5} = \dfrac{2}{5}$.

questions.solution_md: With no common card, the two probabilities simply add.

marking_scheme.step: n(A) = 3, n(B) = 3 and A and B share no card

questions.stem_md:
Two fair dice are thrown together. Let $A$ be "the sum of the numbers is a multiple of $3$" and $B$ "the product of the numbers is odd".

(a) Write down $n(S)$, $n(A)$ and $n(B)$.

(b) List the outcomes of $A \cap B$.

(c) Use the addition theorem to find $P(A \cup B)$ and confirm it by counting $A \cup B$ directly.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $n(S) = 36$. A sum of $3, 6, 9, 12$ occurs in $2 + 5 + 4 + 1 = 12$ ways, so $n(A) = 12$. A product is odd only when both numbers are odd, so $n(B) = 3 \times 3 = 9$.

(b) Both odd with a sum that is a multiple of $3$: $(1, 5), (3, 3), (5, 1)$, so $n(A \cap B) = 3$.

(c) $P(A \cup B) = \dfrac{12}{36} + \dfrac{9}{36} - \dfrac{3}{36} = \dfrac{18}{36} = \dfrac{1}{2}$.

Direct count: $12 + 9 - 3 = 18$ outcomes lie in $A$ or $B$, and $\dfrac{18}{36} = \dfrac{1}{2}$ again.

questions.stem_md:
Five members of an imagined chess club, labelled $A, B, C, D, E$, are available for a demonstration game. Two of them are chosen together, every pair being equally likely. Let $X$ be "member $B$ is chosen" and $Y$ be "neither $A$ nor $E$ is chosen".

(a) List the sample space and state $n(S)$.

(b) List the events $X$, $Y$ and $X \cap Y$.

(c) Find $P(X \cup Y)$ and $P(X' \cap Y')$, and say whether $X$ and $Y$ are mutually exclusive.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $S = \{AB, AC, AD, AE, BC, BD, BE, CD, CE, DE\}$ and $n(S) = 10$.

(b) $X = \{AB, BC, BD, BE\}$ with $n(X) = 4$. For $Y$ the pair must come from $\{B, C, D\}$: $Y = \{BC, BD, CD\}$ with $n(Y) = 3$. Common pairs: $X \cap Y = \{BC, BD\}$, so $n(X \cap Y) = 2$.

(c) $P(X \cup Y) = \dfrac{4 + 3 - 2}{10} = \dfrac{5}{10} = \dfrac{1}{2}$, and $P(X' \cap Y') = 1 - \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}$.

$X \cap Y \ne \varnothing$, so $X$ and $Y$ are not mutually exclusive.

questions.stem_md:
A bag has twelve tickets numbered $1$ to $12$, and one ticket is drawn at random. Let $E_1$, $E_2$, $E_3$ be the events "the number leaves remainder $0$, $1$, $2$ on division by $3$", and let $A$ be "the number is even".

(a) List $E_1$, $E_2$, $E_3$ and show that they are pairwise mutually exclusive and together exhaustive.

(b) Find $P(E_1)$, $P(E_2)$, $P(E_3)$ and their sum.

(c) List $A \cap E_1$, $A \cap E_2$, $A \cap E_3$ and use axiom 3 to find $P(A)$; confirm by counting $A$.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $E_1 = \{3, 6, 9, 12\}$, $E_2 = \{1, 4, 7, 10\}$, $E_3 = \{2, 5, 8, 11\}$. No number lies in two of them, so they are pairwise mutually exclusive, and together they contain all $12$ numbers, so $E_1 \cup E_2 \cup E_3 = S$.

(b) Each has $4$ outcomes, so each has probability $\dfrac{4}{12} = \dfrac{1}{3}$, and the sum is $\dfrac{1}{3} + \dfrac{1}{3} + \dfrac{1}{3} = 1$.

(c) $A \cap E_1 = \{6, 12\}$, $A \cap E_2 = \{4, 10\}$, $A \cap E_3 = \{2, 8\}$. These are mutually exclusive and their union is $A$, so $P(A) = \dfrac{2}{12} + \dfrac{2}{12} + \dfrac{2}{12} = \dfrac{6}{12} = \dfrac{1}{2}$. Counting $A = \{2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12\}$ gives $\dfrac{6}{12}$ as well.

questions.stem_md:
A box holds twenty tokens numbered $1$ to $20$, and one token is drawn at random. Let $A$ be "the number is a multiple of $2$" and $B$ "the number is a multiple of $3$".

(a) Find $n(A)$, $n(B)$ and list $A \cap B$.

(b) Find $P(A \cup B)$ and the probability that the number is a multiple of neither $2$ nor $3$.

(c) Find the probability that the number is a multiple of exactly one of $2$ and $3$.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $A$ has $10$ numbers and $B = \{3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18\}$ has $6$. The common multiples are the multiples of $6$: $A \cap B = \{6, 12, 18\}$, so $n(A \cap B) = 3$.

(b) $P(A \cup B) = \dfrac{10 + 6 - 3}{20} = \dfrac{13}{20}$. The probability of neither is $1 - \dfrac{13}{20} = \dfrac{7}{20}$.

(c) Exactly one means $A \cup B$ without $A \cap B$: $P = \dfrac{13}{20} - \dfrac{3}{20} = \dfrac{10}{20} = \dfrac{1}{2}$. Check: $A$ only has $7$ numbers and $B$ only has $3$, and $\dfrac{7 + 3}{20} = \dfrac{1}{2}$.

questions.solution_md: Exactly one is the union minus the overlap, or the two one-sided parts added.

questions.stem_md:
A die is loaded so that the probability of showing $k$ is $\dfrac{k}{21}$ for $k = 1, 2, \ldots, 6$.

(a) Show that this is a valid probability assignment.

(b) Let $E$ be "an even number" and $F$ "a prime number". Find $P(E)$, $P(F)$ and $P(E \cap F)$.

(c) Find $P(E \cup F)$ by the addition theorem, verify it by adding outcomes, and find the probability of a number that is neither even nor prime.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Every $\dfrac{k}{21}$ is positive, and $\dfrac{1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6}{21} = \dfrac{21}{21} = 1$, so axioms 1 and 2 hold.

(b) $E = \{2, 4, 6\}$: $P(E) = \dfrac{2 + 4 + 6}{21} = \dfrac{12}{21} = \dfrac{4}{7}$. $F = \{2, 3, 5\}$: $P(F) = \dfrac{2 + 3 + 5}{21} = \dfrac{10}{21}$. Only $2$ is both, so $P(E \cap F) = \dfrac{2}{21}$.

(c) $P(E \cup F) = \dfrac{12}{21} + \dfrac{10}{21} - \dfrac{2}{21} = \dfrac{20}{21}$. Check: $E \cup F = \{2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}$ and $\dfrac{2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6}{21} = \dfrac{20}{21}$.

The only number that is neither is $1$, with probability $\dfrac{1}{21} = 1 - \dfrac{20}{21}$.

questions.solution_md: Weighted outcomes: an event probability is the sum of its outcome probabilities.

marking_scheme.step: P(E or F) = 12/21 + 10/21 - 2/21 = 20/21, verified by adding outcomes

questions.stem_md:
In an imagined survey of $200$ households, $120$ own a bicycle, $90$ own a scooter and $40$ own both. A household is chosen at random. Find the probability that it owns

(a) a bicycle or a scooter,

(b) neither a bicycle nor a scooter,

(c) exactly one of the two, and

(d) a bicycle but not a scooter.

answer.model_answer_md:
Let $B$ be "owns a bicycle" and $S$ be "owns a scooter". $P(B) = \dfrac{120}{200}$, $P(S) = \dfrac{90}{200}$ and $P(B \cap S) = \dfrac{40}{200}$.

(a) $P(B \cup S) = \dfrac{120 + 90 - 40}{200} = \dfrac{170}{200} = \dfrac{17}{20}$.

(b) $P(\text{neither}) = 1 - \dfrac{17}{20} = \dfrac{3}{20}$, which is $30$ households.

(c) $P(\text{exactly one}) = \dfrac{170}{200} - \dfrac{40}{200} = \dfrac{130}{200} = \dfrac{13}{20}$.

(d) $P(B \cap S') = \dfrac{120 - 40}{200} = \dfrac{80}{200} = \dfrac{2}{5}$.

questions.solution_md: Counts and probabilities are linked by dividing by the 200 households.
